sections.description: Mendel's peas offered two alleles per gene, one visibly dominant.

sections.description: The population-genetics lesson owns the Hardy-Weinberg law and the forces that move allele frequencies — selection, drift, gene flow, coalescence.

sections.description: Natural selection, as the natural-selection lesson established, is a struggle for existence: differential survival.

sections.description: A confident theory hides its anomalies; Darwin’s sixth chapter walks straight at them.

sections.description: If each species were designed for its habitat, the map of life should track the map of climate.

sections.title: From Lucy to Us: The Story of Human Evolution
sections.description: Somewhere between six and seven million years ago, an African ape population split in two: one branch leads to today's chimpanzees and bonobos, the other to every human being who has ever lived.

sections.title: Biological Classification: The Five Kingdoms and Beyond
sections.description: Biologists have formally described fewer than two million species, and the working guesses for the planet’s total run to eight or ten million.

sections.title: The Plant Kingdom: Algae to Angiosperms
sections.description: Plants were not always landlocked, flower-bearing giants.

sections.title: Classification as Genealogy: Homology, Analogy and Rudimentary Organs
sections.description: The classification lesson in this chapter owns the filing cabinet: binomial names, the taxonomic hierarchy, Whittaker’s kingdoms, the three domains.

sections.title: The Flowering Plant Body: Morphology and Anatomy
sections.description: A flowering plant looks simple — roots below, shoot above, leaves in between — but every exam board expects you to read this body like an engineer: which root stores food, which stem climbs, why…

sections.title: Photosynthesis: Light and Dark Reactions
sections.description: Photosynthesis converts light energy into chemical energy and feeds nearly every food web on Earth.

sections.title: Plant Physiology: How Plants Actually Work
sections.description: Photosynthesis gets the glory, but a plant's real engineering problem is plumbing.

sections.title: Plant Reproduction: Flowers, Pollination and Seeds
sections.description: A flower is not decoration — it is a reproductive machine of packaged gametes, built to trade pollen with the world.

sections.title: Inside the Seed: Grain Anatomy, Dormancy and the Germination Trigger
sections.description: The reproduction lesson ended where double fertilization ends: a seed with coat, stored food and embryo, development paused.

sections.title: Animal Tissue Types: Four Families, One Body Plan
sections.description: Organs look like improvisations, but histology reveals the trick: only four tissue families do all the work.

sections.title: The Animal Kingdom: A Tour of Body Plans and Phyla
sections.description: Animals are multicellular consumers — they eat other organisms, lack the rigid walls and chloroplasts of plants, and bind their cells together with the protein collagen.

sections.title: Animal Behavior: Instinct, Learning, Signals
sections.description: A greylag goose rolls a displaced egg back into her nest with her beak — and if a researcher swipes the egg away mid-motion, she completes the whole maneuver on empty ground.

sections.title: How Animals Sense the World
sections.description: Ask what a dog smells on a lamppost and you brush a bigger question: what is it like to be another animal?

sections.title: Life at the Limits: How Organisms Answer Habitat and Abiotic Stress
sections.description: Every organism on Earth runs the same core business — keeping its internal chemistry within viable bounds — while the world outside swings between freezing and scorching, flood and drought, noon…

sections.title: Populations and Communities: Interactions, Niches and Disturbance
sections.description: Ecology is biology with the walls removed: organisms living not as specimens but as members of populations, and populations woven into communities.

sections.title: Ecosystems and the Flow of Energy
sections.description: A hectare of grassland intercepts a flood of sunlight, yet only a sliver ever becomes rabbit.

sections.title: Food Webs and Trophic Cascades: Who Eats Whom, and Why It Matters
sections.description: Draw a food chain — grass, antelope, lion — and you have sketched a cartoon.

sections.title: Biomes: A Tour of Earth's Major Ecosystems
sections.description: Why do the same latitudes of North America, Asia, and Europe grow the same forests, thousands of kilometers apart?

sections.title: Population Ecology: Growth, Limits and Cycles
sections.description: A population is all the individuals of one species in one place, and population ecology is the accounting that predicts whether that number will explode, crash, or settle into balance.

sections.title: Brazilian Biomes and the Geography of Deforestation

sections.title: Biodiversity and the Sixth Extinction
sections.description: Life on Earth has endured five mass extinctions — the worst, at the end of the Permian 252 million years ago, erased roughly 90 percent of marine species.

sections.title: Restoration and Rewilding: Putting Ecosystems Back Together
sections.description: Conservation has two jobs: protect what remains, and put back what was lost.

sections.title: Measuring Biodiversity: Richness, Evenness, Sampling and Simpson’s Index
sections.description: You cannot protect what you cannot count.

sections.title: Bacteria, Viruses, Fungi: A Field Guide to the Microbial World
sections.description: Your body carries more microbial cells than it has human ones, and the world beyond carries more still.

sections.title: Antibiotics and the Rise of Resistance
sections.description: In 1943 a rose thorn could kill; by 1960 penicillin had made such deaths a rarity.

sections.title: The Microbiome: Your Trillion Tenants
sections.description: You are outnumbered in your own body.

sections.title: The Immune System: Innate to Adaptive Defense
sections.description: Your body runs an open-border policy — food, air, cuts, kisses — and still keeps some thirty trillion of its own cells under protection.

sections.title: Autoimmunity and Allergy: When the Defense Misfires
sections.description: The immune system's hardest job is not killing pathogens; it is sparing the self.

sections.title: The Heart and Circulation: One Pump, Two Circuits
sections.description: Every minute, a fist-sized muscle drives roughly five liters of blood through a vessel network that, laid end to end, would circle the Earth two and a half times.

sections.title: Breathing and Gas Exchange: From Air to Cell
sections.description: You can hold your breath for a minute, but the body will not allow two: every cell runs on oxygen delivered moment to moment.

sections.title: The Digestive System: From Meal to Molecule
sections.description: A sandwich is worthless to your cells until it has been dismantled.

sections.title: Kidneys, Hormones and the Body's Balance
sections.description: Two fist-sized kidneys filter roughly 180 liters of fluid from your blood each day — the entire plasma volume dozens of times over — deciding ion by ion what to keep and what to discard.

sections.title: Muscles, Bones and the Machinery of Movement
sections.description: Take one step and a committee of 206 bones, a hundred movable joints, and more than 600 skeletal muscles fires in sequence — a machine that also happens to be alive, self-repairing, and rebuilt…

sections.title: The Endocrine System: Hormones as the Body's Slow Messengers
sections.description: Nerves shout; hormones whisper.

sections.title: The Nervous System: The Body's Command Network
sections.description: Between reading this sentence and scratching an itch, one network sensed, planned, commanded, and corrected the motion.

sections.title: The Senses: How the Body Reads the World
sections.description: You have never actually seen the world — only your brain's reconstruction of it.

sections.title: When Organs Fail: Hearing, Vision and Kidney Technologies

sections.title: Morphogenesis: The Cell Behaviors That Fold, Tube and Sculpt the Embryo
sections.description: Telling an embryo what to build is one problem; actually building it is another.

sections.title: Evo-Devo: How Development Evolves
sections.description: The previous lessons of this book explained how a single body gets built: gradients read, germ layers folded, segments given identity.

sections.title: Marine Biology: Life in the Ocean

sections.title: From Tidepools to Reefs: Coastal Habitats and Communities
sections.description: The Blue Realm chapter described the ocean by depth and light; this lesson walks the shoreline, where the ocean’s productivity and most of its human contact concentrate.

sections.title: Plankton and Larvae: The Drifting Majority of Ocean Life
sections.description: Ask most people to picture ocean life and they imagine fish, whales, coral reefs.

sections.title: Fisheries, Aquaculture and the Future of Ocean Food
sections.description: The ocean-supper lesson painted the marine food web from plankton to apex predators; this topic follows humanity’s place in it.

sections.description: Every species carries a written record of its ancestry, and phylogenetics is the discipline that reads it.

sections.description: The algorithms of bioinformatics — alignment, assembly, tree-building — operate on data that has to live somewhere, in some format, under some identifier scheme.

sections.title: Why Weather Happens: The Atmosphere at Work
sections.description: Weather is the atmosphere rearranging heat.

sections.description: A healthy soil is not dirt but a living ecosystem — minerals, organic matter, roots, fungi, bacteria and animals — that cycles nutrients, stores water and resists erosion.

sections.description: Every hour, more energy from sunlight reaches Earth than humanity uses in a year.

sections.title: Wind Energy: Turbines, Farms and the Physics of Harvesting Wind
sections.description: Wind is second-hand sunlight: the sun heats land and sea unevenly, pressure differences try to even things out, and air rushes from one place to another.

sections.title: Nuclear Energy: Fission Today, Fusion Tomorrow
sections.description: The solar and wind chapters covered the technologies growing fastest; this chapter covers the one already carrying the largest firm low-carbon share.

sections.title: Diabetes and Metabolic Health: When Blood Sugar Runs Off the Rails

sections.description: Your body is more than half water, and every water molecule carries hydrogen nuclei — protons that behave like microscopic compass needles.
